knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")

The primary `statnnet` workflow selects a parsimonious network before
constructing regression-style summaries. This vignette uses the bundled Auto
MPG data and keeps the selection settings deliberately small so that it can be
rebuilt quickly during package checks.

```{r setup, message = FALSE}
library(nnet)
library(statnnet)

data("auto_mpg", package = "statnnet")

analysis_data <- auto_mpg
continuous_variables <- c(
  "mpg", "displacement", "horsepower", "weight", "acceleration",
  "model_year"
)
analysis_data[continuous_variables] <- scale(
  analysis_data[continuous_variables]
)
```

## Select inputs and hidden-layer size

`select_nnet()` alternates between hidden-layer and input selection using an
information criterion. Formula terms are selected as groups, so the indicator
columns for a factor enter or leave together. Multiple starting values are
used for every candidate model; only converged starts are eligible for
selection.

```{r select}
selection <- select_nnet(
  mpg ~ cylinders + displacement + horsepower + weight + acceleration +
    model_year + origin,
  data = analysis_data,
  max_size = 2,
  n_starts = 3,
  criterion = "BIC",
  maxit = 1000,
  seed = 2026,
  progress = FALSE
)

selection
summary(selection)
```

The complete evaluated path remains available for auditing or plotting.

```{r path, fig.alt = "BIC values for the candidate neural-network models evaluated during selection."}
head(selection_path(selection))
plot(selection)
```

## Separate numerical diagnostics from calibration

Converting the result directly with `statnnet()` validates the selected native
`nnet` fit and reports whether covariance-based summaries are numerically
available. The selection itself is unpenalised; a converged fit can still have
poorly conditioned curvature.

Numerical availability is a computational diagnostic, not evidence that Wald
p-values or delta-method intervals have their nominal frequentist coverage.
The Gaussian-response simulations motivating the interface favour
parsimonious networks, including a hidden layer no larger than the fitted input
layer. `statnnet()` records this comparison and warns when there are more
hidden nodes than input nodes. The reported inferential quantities remain
approximate and are empirically supported only under the regimes studied.

The package can calculate the same summaries for supported binary-response
fits, but the package authors have not established their frequentist
calibration; binary Wald tests and intervals should therefore be treated as
exploratory.

```{r diagnose}
selected_model <- suppressWarnings(statnnet(selection))
selected_model
```

Here we refit the selected architecture with a small, pre-specified decay to
demonstrate the inferential interface. This decay value is not selected by
BIC. In an analysis it should be justified and examined in a sensitivity
analysis, while the resulting uncertainty remains conditional on the selected
structure, penalty, and local optimum.

```{r refit}
regularised_fit <- nnet(
  selection$formula,
  data = analysis_data,
  size = selection$size,
  linout = TRUE,
  decay = 0.02,
  Hess = TRUE,
  Wts = selection$fit$wts,
  maxit = 1000,
  trace = FALSE
)

model <- statnnet(
  regularised_fit,
  data = analysis_data,
  response = "continuous"
)

model
summary(model, effects = "none")
anova(model)
```

## Describe the fitted response surface

`pce()` calculates finite differences of the partial-dependence function.
These are descriptive summaries of the fitted network rather than causal
effects, and their pointwise intervals are conditional on the modelling
choices above.

```{r pce}
pce(model, "weight", length_out = 5)
```

```{r pce-plot, fig.alt = "Partial covariate-effect curve for standardized vehicle weight in the selected Auto MPG network."}
plot(model, "weight", length_out = 25)
```

The selected model retains the original `nnet` fit, so ordinary predictions
remain available through `predict()`.

```{r predict}
head(predict(model, newdata = analysis_data))
```
